messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 58
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bomb Disposal Technician
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips, Children Present: Being around children
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Harpreet Singh is a 58-year-old married Sikh man of Punjabi descent who has spent the better part of three decades as a bomb disposal technician. He is a man who has, by professional definition, learned to hold steady in the presence of catastrophic threat. Colleagues have described him as unflappable. He has described himself, until recently, the same way. What brought him to the clinic was not a device in a field or a wire beneath a road. It was his seven-year-old grandson's face, glimpsed at a school pickup, that sent him to his car shaking and unable to drive.

Fourteen months ago, Harpreet's nine-year-old son Rajan — a late child from his second marriage — was admitted to the hospital following a rapid-onset bacterial infection that progressed within hours to septic shock. Harpreet arrived at the emergency department to find Rajan already unconscious, a drip line taped into the crook of his small arm, a nurse adjusting a syringe at the IV port. The room carried the sharp, clean smell of antiseptic that Harpreet would later say seemed to coat the inside of his nose for days afterward. For six hours, the medical team told him and his wife Simran almost nothing definitive. Rajan survived. His recovery was slow but complete. By most measures, the story ended well.

What did not end was Harpreet's experience of those six hours.

In the weeks that followed Rajan's discharge, Harpreet noticed that certain things returned him to that emergency bay with a totality that he could not explain or control. The smell of the hospital antiseptic — encountered at a pharmacy, at a colleague's injury debrief, once simply from a packet of sterile wipes opened in a break room — would deposit him back at Rajan's bedside without passage of time or warning. The memories arrived not as recollections but as images, vivid and immediate: the pale blue of the IV line, the needle sliding beneath Rajan's skin, the particular fluorescent quality of the light. When something in his surroundings triggered this return, his body responded as though the event were current — heart rate surging, hands unsteady, a wave of fear and then a flooding shame at the fear itself.

The shame mattered to Harpreet enormously. He had spent his career training himself to act under conditions that would incapacitate most people, and he had come to believe that what was happening to him now was evidence of a fundamental weakness he had not previously known was there. He was increasingly certain that the intensity and strangeness of his reactions — the way a smell could erase thirty years of professional composure — meant that something in him had broken in a way that was not recoverable. He feared, though he had not said this aloud until his intake session, that he was losing his mind.

He began sleeping poorly, lying awake in a state of readiness he could not switch off, as though some part of him remained posted at a threshold waiting for the next emergency. At work, his unit occasionally handled scenes near schools or community centres, and the presence of children nearby — their voices, their proximity — had become its own source of acute distress. He had begun requesting reassignment away from such callouts, offering technical justifications to his supervisor. His supervisor had noticed the pattern. A formal review of his fitness for operational duties had been quietly initiated, and it was this — the professional consequence, the prospect of losing the identity he had built across three decades — that finally brought him through the clinic door.

What Harpreet most fears is that the review will confirm what he already suspects about himself: that he is not the man he believed himself to be, and that nothing that has happened to him since Rajan's illness can be undone. What he hopes for, stated quietly at the end of the intake session, is simply to be able to stand in a room with his son without bracing for disaster.
